content: Osteoporosis, a condition characterized by impaired bone mineralization, affects approximately one-third of adults with cystic fibrosis. Bisphosphonates are medications known to enhance bone mineral density and reduce the risk of fractures in postmenopausal women and individuals on long-term oral corticosteroids. This review aimed to evaluate the effects of bisphosphonates on fracture frequency, bone mineral density, quality of life, adverse events, trial withdrawals, and survival in individuals with cystic fibrosis. The review included nine randomized controlled trials involving 385 participants, comprising 272 adults and 113 children aged 5 to 18 years. The duration of these trials ranged from six months to two years. Only two of the studies were deemed to have a low risk of bias across all domains. Bisphosphonates in Adults with Cystic Fibrosis (No Lung Transplantation) Seven trials focused on adults without lung transplants, while one trial included both adults and children without lung transplants. A total of 238 adults and 113 children were analyzed separately. Among adults, three trials investigated intravenous bisphosphonates (pamidronate in one trial and zoledronate in two trials), while five trials assessed oral bisphosphonates (risedronate in one trial and alendronate in four trials). Comparisons were made against placebo or calcium (with or without vitamin D). Fractures: At 12 months, there was no significant difference between bisphosphonates and control groups in the occurrence of new vertebral fractures (odds ratio [OR] 0.22, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.02 to 2.09; very low-certainty evidence). Two trials reported no vertebral fractures at 24 months. Similarly, no differences were observed in non-vertebral fractures at 12 months (OR 2.11, 95% CI 0.18 to 25.35; very low-certainty evidence), and no non-vertebral fractures were reported at 24 months in two trials. Total fracture rates also showed no differences at 12 months (OR 0.57, 95% CI 0.13 to 2.50), with no fractures reported at 24 months in two trials. Bone Mineral Density: Bisphosphonates may increase bone mineral density at the lumbar spine (mean difference [MD] 6.31, 95% CI 5.39 to 7.22; low-certainty evidence) and at the hip or femur (MD 4.41, 95% CI 3.44 to 5.37; low-certainty evidence) at 12 months. Quality of Life: There was no clear difference in quality of life scores at 12 months (low-certainty evidence). Adverse Events: Bisphosphonates were associated with a higher likelihood of adverse events, particularly bone pain, at 12 months (OR 8.49, 95% CI 3.20 to 22.56; moderate-certainty evidence). Bisphosphonates in Children with Cystic Fibrosis (No Lung Transplantation) One trial involving 113 children compared oral alendronate to placebo. All evidence was graded as low certainty. Fractures: At 12 months, there were no significant differences between treatment and placebo groups in new vertebral fractures (OR 0.32, 95% CI 0.03 to 3.13), non-vertebral fractures (OR 0.19, 95% CI 0.01 to 4.04), or total fractures (OR 0.18, 95% CI 0.02 to 1.61). Bone Mineral Density: Bisphosphonates may increase bone mineral density at the lumbar spine at 12 months (MD 14.50, 95% CI 12.91 to 16.09). Adverse Events: There were no significant differences in bone or muscle pain, fever, or gastrointestinal adverse events between groups. The trial did not measure bone mineral density at the hip/femur or assess quality of life. Bisphosphonates in Adults with Cystic Fibrosis (Post-Lung Transplantation) One trial involving 34 adults who had undergone lung transplantation compared intravenous pamidronate to no bisphosphonate treatment. Data were reported at 24 months. Fractures: There were no differences in the number of vertebral or non-vertebral fractures between groups. Bone Mineral Density: Treatment with bisphosphonates increased bone mineral density at the lumbar spine (MD 6.20, 95% CI 4.28 to 8.12) and femur (MD 7.90, 95% CI 5.78 to 10.02). Adverse Events: No participants in either group reported bone pain or fever. Quality of life was not assessed. Conclusions Oral and intravenous bisphosphonates may improve bone mineral density in individuals with cystic fibrosis. However, there is insufficient evidence to determine whether these treatments reduce fracture rates. Intravenous bisphosphonates may cause severe bone pain and flu-like symptoms. Larger, longer-duration trials, including pediatric populations, are needed to evaluate the effects of bisphosphonates on fracture rates, survival, and adverse events. Future studies should also investigate whether corticosteroids can mitigate adverse effects and assess gastrointestinal side effects associated with oral bisphosphonates.
